world_status: statement found in a copy already on file

earlier_scan.source_named: Sandefur, John R. 1979. An Australian Creole in the Northern Territory: a description of Ngukurr-Bamyili dialects (SIL-AAB); APiCS survey chapter (checked online: no stress section).

new_statements.quote: Stress is not written either in the Northern Territory orthography or in this monograph. The general tendency is that Kriol follows the traditional languages and stresses the first syllable in words of two or more syllables as in: kápardi 'drink of tea, mid-work break' núgudwan 'bad, useless' búrluman 'cattle (singular)'. Some words retain the stress pattern of the English etymon particularly those which in English begin with a consonant cluster. blanket > bilángkirr sleep > silíp Others vary according to the speaker and the 'light' versus 'heavy' varieties.
new_statements.citation: Hudson, Joyce. 1983 [reprinted 1985]. Grammatical and semantic aspects of Fitzroy Valley Kriol. Work Papers of SIL-AAB, Series A, Vol. 8. Darwin: Summer Institute of Linguistics.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2, p. 25 (PDF page 39 of the 'Intro' file)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of words of two or more syllables, following the pattern of the Aboriginal substrate languages. Corroborated for the basilectal Fitzroy Crossing variety by Fraser 1977: 168-169 (all 2- and 3-syllable words initial; 4-syllable words primary on first, secondary on third; stress non-phonemic), and for Roper Kriol by Bundgaard-Nielsen & Baker 2015: 3 ('All words had initial stress').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Hudson says nothing. Fraser 1977: 168-169 (Fitzroy Crossing basilect): secondary stress 'rarely noted and then only on four-syllable words', usually on the third syllable (mintupala 'we (1du.excl)', lipaRinka 'Liveringa'), occasionally on the final syllable (makeRamap 'to mess up'); cue is slightly higher pitch, primary stress cue is loudness.
new_statements.exceptions: Some words retain the stress of the English etymon, especially those whose English source begins with a consonant cluster and receives an epenthetic vowel (bilángkirr 'blanket', silíp 'sleep'); other words vary by speaker and by 'light' (acrolectal) vs 'heavy' (basilectal) variety (purdéita ~ purdeita 'potato', banana ~ banana, p. 26). Fraser 1977: 169 adds that in prepause emphatic and question intonation contours the final syllable takes primary stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for Fitzroy Valley Kriol (Kimberley, WA) across the light/heavy continuum; Fraser's statement is for the phonological word in the basilect, with separate phrase-final intonational effects. The Roper (Northern Territory) dialects have no published stress rule of their own: Sandefur 1979 defers intonation/rhythm, Sandefur 1986 says suprasegmental phonology has 'yet to be undertaken', and APiCS 2013 says Kriol prosody 'has not been described'; the only Roper evidence is the instrumental note that all stimulus words had initial stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both first-hand stress statements describe the Fitzroy Valley (Kimberley, Western Australia) dialect: Hudson 1983/1985 = Fitzroy Valley Kriol across the light/heavy continuum; Fraser 1977 = 'Fitzroy Crossing Children's Pidgin', the basilectal Fitzroy Crossing variety. Glottolog 5.x krio1252 has no dialect-level glottocodes (child_dialect_count 0), so these fall under krio1252 itself; Hudson 1985 is listed in krio1252's references. The core Roper River / Ngukurr-Barunga (NT) dialects have no published word-stress rule found; the only Roper evidence is Bundgaard-Nielsen & Baker 2015 (ICPhS) noting that all their stimulus words had initial stress. Gurindji Kriol (Meakins 2007, in the Glottolog list) is a separate mixed language (guri1249) and was not used.

sources.note: Ch. 2 'Sound system' and ch. 3 orthography contain no stress rule; the volume introduction states 'Intonation and rhythm, word formation... are not discussed' (deferred to a Part 2 that did not appear). Only incidental mention: in a derivation example, 'the vowel in the unstressed (second) syllable changed to conform to that in the stressed (first) syllable' (/burom/ > /bulum/ 'from'), implying initial stress.
